content: The systematic review identified a significant reduction in cryptococcal disease among individuals living with HIV who have low CD4 cell counts, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 12% to 89%. Additionally, a 71% reduction in the incidence of cryptococcal disease was observed. While the incidence of serious adverse events did not differ significantly, there was some evidence suggesting an increased risk of fluconazole-resistant Candida infections. National guidelines should determine the optimal duration of prophylaxis based on available resources. The duration of fluconazole primary prophylaxis varied across randomized trials that demonstrated the clinical benefits of this intervention. For instance, in the REALITY trial conducted in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, fluconazole (100 mg once daily) was discontinued after 12 weeks. In another trial conducted in Uganda during the era of antiretroviral therapy (ART), fluconazole (200 mg three times per week) was discontinued when participants’ CD4 cell counts reached 200 cells/mm³. The recommendations outlined apply to adults and adolescents with advanced HIV disease. However, these recommendations were not extended to children due to the rarity of cryptococcal disease in this age group, even in high-incidence countries. The 2022 guidelines introduced a new recommendation for the preferred antifungal regimen during the induction phase of treatment. The 2018 WHO guidelines recommended a seven-day course of amphotericin B deoxycholate combined with flucytosine, followed by seven days of fluconazole (1200 mg daily), as the preferred induction regimen for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This recommendation was based on moderate-certainty evidence for adults and low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents. Liposomal amphotericin B was preferred over amphotericin B deoxycholate due to its better tolerability. Alternative options were also recommended based on the availability of treatments. If flucytosine was unavailable, a 14-day regimen of amphotericin B deoxycholate plus fluconazole was recommended. If amphotericin B deoxycholate was unavailable, an oral 14-day regimen of flucytosine and fluconazole was recommended. These recommendations applied to all age groups and settings, with observational data supporting the use of amphotericin B and flucytosine in children. Amphotericin B deoxycholate is associated with several side effects, including anemia, nausea, vomiting, rigors, fever, blood pressure fluctuations, hypoxia, and metabolic disturbances such as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and nephrotoxicity. The 2018 WHO guidelines noted that liposomal amphotericin B was preferred due to equivalent efficacy and better safety. However, access to liposomal amphotericin B remains extremely limited in lowand middle-income countries due to its high cost, lack of registration, limited manufacturers, and the need for close monitoring during intravenous administration. A single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B-based regimen, tested in a large Phase III trial, offers an additional option. Access to flucytosine is also limited in these settings. The 2022 guidelines recommend a single high dose (10 mg/kg) of liposomal amphotericin B combined with 14 days of flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day, divided into four doses) and fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents, up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) as the preferred induction regimen for treating cryptococcal meningitis. This recommendation is supported by moderate-certainty evidence for adults and low-certainty evidence for children. Alternative induction regimens are recommended if liposomal amphotericin B is unavailable. These include a seven-day course of amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg per day) with flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day, divided into four doses), followed by seven days of fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults and 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents, up to a maximum of 800 mg daily). If no amphotericin B formulations are available, a 14-day regimen of fluconazole (1200 mg daily, 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents) combined with flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day, divided into four doses) is recommended. Fluconazole and flucytosine is the only recommended oral combination regimen and has been associated with lower mortality compared to amphotericin B deoxycholate plus fluconazole. If flucytosine is unavailable, a 14-day regimen of liposomal amphotericin B (3–4 mg/kg per day) plus fluconazole (1200 mg daily, 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents, up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) is recommended. The systematic review from 2022 identified a randomized trial comparing a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B combined with oral flucytosine and fluconazole for 14 days to the 2018 WHO-recommended induction therapy. The trial, conducted in Botswana, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, enrolled 844 individuals with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 10 weeks, with the trial powered to demonstrate non-inferiority at a 10% margin. The single high-dose regimen showed fewer potentially life-threatening adverse events compared to the control group. For children, the WHO-convened Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group confirmed that evidence supporting the use of a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B could be extrapolated to children, although the certainty of evidence was downgraded to low due to the lack of direct evidence. The strong recommendation for both adults and children was based on the moderate certainty of evidence for harm reduction and low certainty for mortality reduction. Liposomal amphotericin B has the advantage of single-dose administration and, when combined with flucytosine and fluconazole, is at least as effective as amphotericin B deoxycholate-based combination treatment. It also has a better side-effect profile, with fewer risks related to drug toxicity. Implementing the single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimen could increase access to effective treatment for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, particularly in healthcare facilities unable to procure or safely administer seven or more days of amphotericin B deoxycholate treatment. Amphotericin B formulations, including liposomal, deoxycholate, and lipid complex, are not interchangeable. For cryptococcal meningitis, only amphotericin B deoxycholate and liposomal amphotericin B are recommended. Healthcare providers must avoid mixing up these products, as the doses differ, and significant adverse events have been reported when the deoxycholate formulation was given at higher-than-recommended doses. The single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimen is associated with fewer intravenous doses, reduced need for preand post-hydration, and less intensive monitoring for drug-related toxicity. This regimen may enable rapid hospital discharge for individuals with good clinical status. The favorable safety profile, with a lower risk of anemia and hypokalemia, reduces the intensity of monitoring and management of drug-related toxicity. Cost analyses from the AMBITION trial showed that the mean total costs per person were slightly higher in the liposomal amphotericin B group compared to the control group. However, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was favorable, and cost-effectiveness was robust in sensitivity analyses. Despite the high cost of liposomal amphotericin B, access is expected to improve as generic manufacturers enter the market. Ethical considerations emphasize the need for equitable distribution of the benefits and burdens of public health programs. Liposomal amphotericin B, combined with flucytosine and fluconazole, offers a more accessible and effective treatment option for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, particularly in resource-limited settings.
